https://www.barrons.com/articles/ciena-cfo-talks-cloud-software-and-how-to-think-about-cash-balances-1522091562 Ciena’s CFO on Cloud Computing, Corporate Cash, and Credit Lines By Updated March 26, 2018 3:12 p.m. ET Text Size Large Ciena chief financial officer Jim Moylan. Illustration: Ciena Inc. 
The other day I had lunch with Ciena ( CIEN ) chief financial officer Jim Moylan . Over a nice tuna niçoise, we discussed cloud computing , telcos and the outlook for Ciena’s chip business. 
Moylan, who at age 67 has been in the job for eleven years, is perhaps the finance equivalent of Paul McCartney to CEO Gary Smith’s John Lennon . 
Moylan has an interesting background for a tech executive, having spent many years working in the energy industry, at Sonat Inc., now a division of Kinder-Morgan Inc. ( KMI ). 
He brought up that experience many times during the course of our lunch, offering a nuanced perspective on how capital and debt work. 
For example, on the matter of cash balances , when I asked how much net cash Ciena should maintain — some companies such as Apple ( AAPL ) have promised to reduce it to zero , or almost zero — Moylan declined to list a figure or a percentage. Instead, he noted how much cash you keep “is all a matter of access to capital ." 
"Any company of size in the energy business is an investment grade company,” he notes, which has not always been the case for tech. Energy companies "almost always have been run at about a zero cash balance," as a consequence. 
He applauds the recent U.S. tax revamp as changing the focus of companies, with the overall effect that Ciena, and others, will move toward more and more “efficient” balance sheets: Most tech companies, it's interesting, have very large cash balances. This is a business that can be volatile, and traditionally, if you need capital, you sometimes don’t want to have to go to the markets to raise it. And that set of factors was there for us at Ciena. But, we are now in the range of an investment grade rating, and so our need to hold cash is declining. One thing good about this new tax law is, it doesn’t end that need to keep cash on hand, but it makes it much more a business decision, not a tax rate decision. A more-efficient balance sheet is the trend. 
Cloudy future 
In addition to finance we covered several of the big topics that are specifically of interest to Ciena. One is how much more momentum the company has selling fiber-optic gear to operators of cloud computing shops such as Alphabet ’s ( GOOGL ) Google and Amazon ’s ( AMZN ) Amazon Web Services . 
Those kinds of customers made up 15% of Ciena's revenue in the most recent quarter , not counting the indirect ways they also procure from the company. 
Is cloud spending on Ciena gear going to hit a wall? I asked. 
“We don’t feel that way now,” replied Moylan. "They [cloud operators] decided five years ago it was better for them to build out their own connections” rather than to procure big "backbone” pipes from the phone companies. 
"They are the masters of content,” he explains. You know, 90-plus percent of content flows between their data centers. At other end you’ve got the users. Service providers have to build out their metros [metro-area networks, the points that connect to individual Web users.] We are not concerned about concentration, per se, among the cloud-scale customers. As long as demand for data and video is growing, it should be a good market for us for a while. Our dedicated equipment for hyperscale, Wave Server , went from 10 million units in 2016 to 110M last year, so, up significantly. We have 80 customers for that product. It’s lower-priced than what we typically sell to telcos, the 6500 series , but the good thing for us is the margin profile is similar. 
Following from that, I asked if investors should be concerned about the traditional telecom customers. Results from that crowd have been sloppy for a while now, not just for Ciena but for anyone who sells to the telcos. Ciena has contracts with the major operators, including AT&T ( T ) and Verizon Communications ( VZ ) in the U.S. 
Moylan’s response was calm, unruffled, sticking to the big picture: "They have a good future ahead of them as the translation networks, if you will, from content guys down to the end user." 
Moreover, "You want to have them as customers, because the fact they are not growing as rapidly as other customers is a temporary phenomenon, especially given they have to build out 5G [wireless, the next big bump up in speed for telco networks.]" 
"We said 5G is about the densification of the access network, and it’s likely AT&T and Verizon are planning now for that, even if it isn’t as big of a driver for us at the moment." 
The 400G wave 
I asked about the impending arrival of “ 400G ” networking, the next bump-up in speed for data-center connections. There’s some uncertainty on the Street how fast this move to 400 billion bits per second will happen. 
Moylan wasn’t inclined to be very specific, characterizing 400G less as an immediate priority, more as something important to have on the shelf for whenever it takes off in a big way. 
Historically, you know, we have been first to market with each capacity upgrade shipment. We started shipping [400G] last September or October, and we are still the only ones shipping it in any volume. It’s a proof point for our customers, is one thing. Secondly, the data center guys' [cloud operators like Google] demand for bandwidth is insatiable. This year all, over half of our capacity will be in 100G, and the rest will be 200G, or lower-speed gear." 
A brand new chip business 
I asked when the company will give more granular detail on its chip business, which the company last year started selling for the first time as an stand-alone part to competing fiber gear vendors. 
“We don’t have any POs yet,” or purchase orders, for the chip, "WaveLogic A.I.,” he said. 
"Even in a three-year plan for it, we don’t have a big expectation for the take-up there in terms of revenue." 
So why even make the effort? I asked. 
Why not? was basically Moylan’s response. "When you look at an optical system, every optical system has some essential parts. It has a modem, with a chip and a laser, and some software." 
“So, we thought to ourselves, there was probably roughly a billion dollars sold of the silicon, of which our captive sales, sales for just our gear, are maybe 15%. We said, there is potential upside there if we can capture some of the 85% that is the rest of the industry’s silicon need." 
The services business 
Ciena has increasingly made a push into software , which brings higher profit margin. Is there a risk, I asked, that the software it is selling to “automate” the management of customers' networks will drive down the revenue that Ciena traditionally gets to help manage those networks, reported as services sales. 
"I don’t think so,” he replied. 
"We have three basic elements to our services business, which are deployment of the network, consulting on the architecture of the network, and then the maintenance of that network. You will always need to have some degree of all three, because these are extremely complicated, complex systems. So, I don’t think automation really ends up affecting any of those in any meaningful way. 
How ‘bout some KPIs? 
I asked Moylan, as he’s boosting the company’s software, why he doesn’t spend more time offering what the Street calls “ key performance indicators ,” or KPIs . 
These non-income-statement numbers are given as kinds of indicators of progress. Microsoft ( MSFT ) CFO Amy Hood has made them very popular among Microsoft investors. 
And Cisco Systems ( CSCO ), which competes with Ciena in some markets, has been increasingly emphasizing its own KPIs as the company shifts to more and more software. See my most recent interview with Cisco’s CFO, Kelly Kramer. 
Moylan nodded and smiled at this, replying “it’s a subject we are talking about internally." 
He went on to say that there are three parts of software for Ciena. The two biggest of those have to do with hardware network management, on the one hand, and the Ciena "domain controller" and upgrades to it. 
"And then, on top of that, there are the advanced applications, our Blue Planet business. Blue Planet has big potential upside for us, but it's still small. We think it’s not too far in the future that it will be a meaningful component of revenue for us." 
“It’s still small for us, so so far, there hasn't been much point in disclosing more about a small thing." 
“Ultimately, the Street wants to know how the new things, such as Blue Planet, translate into the old thing, profitability. We realize that." 
But, "Once you start down a path of disclosure, or tonality, you have to continue on that path,” he observed. Translation: Moylan doesn’t want to start to give more detail, including KPIs, until he’s sure he can consistently and reliably delivery that detail quarter after quarter without fail. 
A history lesson 
Lunch with a CFO can be an education in the arcana of finance. For example, Moylan pointed out that customarily, companies large and small would draw on bank debt in the form of a revolving line of credit , a “revolver." 
The option to draw down that revolver was a nice cushion, he notes, which didn’t have to be carried on the balance sheet. 
But, he observes, banks are less inclined now to do revolvers, "because they have to keep capital to match the value of that revolver." 
"The biggest companies in the world still use revolvers, of course. It’s just an extra line of credit that’s there when they need it." Most Popular
